items.name: Trade by Barter
items.about: Before coins and notes, people in what is now Nigeria traded goods directly for other goods. The CBN lists salt among the earliest items used this way, before 1600, along with beads and other goods. Barter only works when each side wants what the other has, so commodities that everyone valued and could count, such as cowrie shells and metal manillas, came to be used as money. These in turn gave way to British coin from 1880 and West African Currency Board money from 1912.

items.name: Manillas
items.about: Manillas were open, horseshoe-shaped metal rings that served as money in southern Nigeria for over four centuries, and could also be worn as bracelets. Portuguese traders brought them in their hundreds of thousands from the early 1500s, and they became a main currency of the Atlantic slave trade: at Calabar in 1505 an enslaved person cost 8 to 10 manillas. Later the trade moved to palm oil, and English foundries in Bristol and Birmingham made most of the brass rings. The colonial government banned imports in 1902, then in 1948 bought back over 32 million manillas in Operation Manilla and sold them as scrap metal. They stopped being legal tender on 1 April 1949, though families could keep up to 200 for weddings and funerals.

items.name: Cowrie Shells
items.about: Cowries are small, glossy sea shells from the Indian Ocean that served as money across much of Nigeria for centuries. They were hard to fake, easy to count and lasted for years, and European ships brought them in huge numbers: at least 30 billion reached the Bight of Benin between 1500 and 1875. Large sums were counted in strings, heads and bags, but the flood of imports pushed their value down, until in 1865 a bag of 20,000 shells was worth only a pound or two in Lagos. British coin and later West African Currency Board money replaced them; cowries were still taken for taxes in parts of British West Africa into the early 20th century, and Wikipedia notes informal use lasting until the 1960s.

items.name: Five Pounds Note (Bank of British West Africa)
items.about: Before the West African Currency Board existed, private banks in Lagos could issue their own notes. The Bank of British West Africa, formed in 1893 from Elder Dempster's banking business, had Bradbury Wilkinson prepare this five pound note for its Lagos branch. The only example on record is a printer's proof, so there is no proof it was ever paid out to the public. The bank later became the Bank of West Africa and then First Bank of Nigeria.

items.name: One Tenth Penny Coin (WACB)
items.about: The one tenth penny was the smallest coin used in colonial Nigeria, made for very small everyday purchases. The first coins of 1907 were struck in light aluminium, but they did not last, and from 1908 the coin was made in cupro-nickel. It kept the same holed design through five reigns: a crown and the ruler's name on one side, a six-pointed star on the other. The word NIGERIA was dropped after 1911, and the last coins, in bronze, are dated 1957.

items.system: British pound sterling / British West African pound
items.about: From 1907 Nigeria had its own penny, a large holed coin made for the colony instead of the British penny. One side carries a crown and the ruler's name with the value in English and Arabic, so it could be read across the region. The other side shows a six-pointed star and, until 1911, the name NIGERIA. When the West African Currency Board took over in 1912 the legend became simply BRITISH WEST AFRICA, and from 1952 the coin was made in bronze until its last date in 1958.

items.name: Emergency Notes 1918
items.about: Late in 1918 two paper one shilling notes were issued in Nigeria as small change. The West African Currency Board issued a one shilling note in Lagos dated 30 November 1918, printed on one side only and showing a coin with a tree. In December 1918 the Government of Nigeria issued its own green one shilling note under Ordinance XXII of 1918, also blank on the back. These are the only 1918 emergency notes found: no emergency notes of other values were found, and the ten and twenty shillings notes dated 30 March 1918 are regular Board issues.

items.name: Half Penny Coin (Nigerian)
items.about: The halfpenny was the smallest coin of Nigeria's own first currency, issued in 1959 as the country prepared for independence. It kept the holed shape of the older British West Africa halfpenny, but no portrait of the Queen appears on it: a crown and her title stand in for her. The value is written in English and Arabic script so that readers of both could use it, and the six-pointed star on the back was Nigeria's emblem at the time. Only the 1959 date was ever struck, and the coin ended when the naira and kobo arrived in 1973.

items.name: One Shilling Coin (Nigerian)
items.about: The shilling was the workhorse coin of the Nigerian pound, worth one-twentieth of a pound. Its back, by Humphrey Paget, shows an oil palm, the tree behind the palm-oil trade that drove much of southern Nigeria's economy. Unlike the other 1959 coins it was struck again after independence, with 1961 and 1962 dates, still under the Federation of Nigeria name and the Queen's portrait. It was withdrawn when the naira replaced the pound in 1973, at 10 kobo to the shilling.

items.name: Five Shillings Note (Nigerian)

The 1958 design shows a river scene, and it carries the 'Federation of Nigeria' name used before the republic. During the civil war a recoloured 1968 version replaced it, and that design lived on almost unchanged as the 50 kobo note of 1973 to 1978.

items.name: Five Shillings Note (Biafran)
items.about: Biafra issued its own notes from 29 January 1968 so it no longer had to rely on Nigerian money during the civil war. The Five Shillings was the lowest note and one of only two values in that first issue, alongside the One Pound. The front shows a palm tree with a rising sun, Biafra's national symbol, and the back shows four Biafran girls. It was printed again in the second issue of February 1969 with new colours and new serial prefixes, and lost all value when Biafra surrendered in January 1970.

items.name: Five Thousand Naira Note (Proposed)
items.about: In August 2012 CBN Governor Sanusi Lamido Sanusi announced a ₦5,000 note for early 2013, part of a plan to redesign the ₦50 to ₦1,000 notes and turn the ₦5, ₦10 and ₦20 into coins. The note was to honour three women activists: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, Margaret Ekpo and Gambo Sawaba. The CBN board and the President had approved the new structure in late 2011. After the Senate and House of Representatives called for it to be dropped, President Goodluck Jonathan suspended the plan in September 2012, and the note was never issued.

items.name: eNaira
items.about: The eNaira is the Central Bank of Nigeria's digital version of the naira, the first central bank digital currency of its kind in Africa. President Muhammadu Buhari launched it on 25 October 2021. Uptake was weak: an IMF review in 2023 found fewer than 1% of active bank accounts signed up and 98.5% of wallets unused in a typical week, despite a USSD option added in 2022 for people without smartphones. By 2025 the app had gone from Google Play, and in June 2026 the CBN said it would reposition the eNaira for government payments to citizens and cross-border transfers.

changes.title: IMF review
changes.what: An IMF paper found adoption 'disappointingly low': about 802,000 transactions since launch and 98.5% of wallets unused in a given week.

changes.title: Went offline
changes.what: The eNaira app was removed from Google Play and the USSD code stopped working; in August the CBN blamed low acceptance and weak awareness.

changes.title: Repositioned
changes.what: The CBN's Payments System Vision 2028 said it would refocus the eNaira on government-to-person and cross-border payments, citing slow adoption.
